A dependant with CAD 16,452 or more of net income: nothing.

A teenager earning CAD 6,000 from a summer job: CAD 10,452, a credit of CAD 1,463.28. The teenager’s pay costs the household CAD 840 of the parent’s federal credit, even though the teenager probably owes no tax on it.

CAD 2,740 is added to the basic personal amount before the dependant’s income is subtracted. For an infirm child of yours under 18, the CAD 2,740 is claimed on line 30500 instead, which does not depend on the child’s income.
Canada child benefit: CCB is based on adjusted family net income and is neither reduced nor increased by this claim; its primary-caregiver rules are separate from the line 30400 tests.

Child support. You generally cannot claim for a child you had to pay support for (subsection 118(5)). The exceptions: when both parents had to pay support for the child, the one the parents agree on may claim; and in the year of a separation part-way through the year, you can choose between claiming line 30400 (plus lines 30425 and 31800 for that child) or deducting support paid to the spouse on line 22000.

Line 30450: someone who cannot claim line 30400 because they have a spouse may still claim the caregiver amount for an infirm dependant 18 or older there. Nobody can claim line 30450 for a dependant already claimed on line 30400.

Line 30500: when a child does not live with both parents, only the parent claiming line 30400 for that child can claim the CAD 2,740 infirm child amount, with exceptions for a parent who claimed line 30300 or line 30400 for someone else.

Line 31800, disability amount transferred from a dependant: claiming, or being able to claim, line 30400 for a dependant is one route to transfer their unused disability amount. The two claims add up.
No income: CAD 16,452, a credit of CAD 2,303.28.

One claim per household. Only one line 30400 claim can be made for a home, even if it has several dependants, and the amount cannot be split. Two siblings sharing an apartment with their mother cannot each claim for her.

One claimant per dependant. If two people could claim for the same dependant and cannot agree, neither can claim. Folio S1-F4-C2 (paragraph 2.57) explains that separated parents who share custody of two or more children may each claim for a different child, provided each meets every condition for that child.
Spouse amount: line 30300 and line 30400 cannot both be claimed. A couple living together claims line 30300, never line 30400, for their child.

A parent or grandparent qualifies at any age without an infirmity. An adult child or sibling qualifies only with one. The dependant generally must live in Canada, but your own child need not, provided they lived with you. The “at any time in the year” wording means a person who separated during the year, or whose child was born during it, can still qualify, provided they do not also claim line 30300. Schedule 5 asks for the date of a change in marital status.

A parent or grandparent with CPP, OAS and a small pension usually exceeds the threshold. A widowed mother with CAD 15,000 of income leaves only CAD 1,452 to claim (CAD 203.28 of credit), and at CAD 16,452 nothing. If she depends on you because of an infirmity, the picture changes, as the next section shows.

A parent who receives support is not barred. The rule turns on who had to pay it under the agreement or order, not on who had the child more often. Where both parents had to pay support for the child, for example under a set-off arrangement, the claim needs both payers’ agreement.

A single parent earning little owes little federal tax after their own basic personal amount, Canada employment amount and CPP and EI credits, so most of the credit is lost: here it is fully usable from about CAD 36,643 of employment income. The credit is non-refundable and unused amounts cannot be carried forward or moved to another person.

A worked guide to line 30400 for 2026: who qualifies as a single claimant and an eligible dependant, the one-claim-per-home and shared-custody rules, the child-support restriction, how every dollar of a dependant’s income reduces the amount, the CAD 2,740 infirmity addition and the line 30425 top-up, why a low-income single parent may not be able to use it, and CRA statistics on who claims. Six charts and an editable model.

Every dollar of a dependant’s net income reduces line 30400 by a dollar. For an infirm dependant 18 or older the line 30425 top-up keeps the total at CAD 8,773 until their income reaches CAD 20,601, then it falls to zero at CAD 29,374, well past the point where line 30400 alone would end. The claimant’s net income of CAD 52,000 sets the basic personal amount used.

Every filer gets the basic personal amount (line 30000). A couple can claim a second one through the spouse or common-law partner amount (line 30300) when one partner supports the other. The amount for an eligible dependant on line 30400, often called the “equivalent-to-spouse” amount, gives the same second amount to a person without a supporting partner who supports a child, parent or other qualifying relative at home.

For 2026 a claimant with no spouse or common-law partner (or one they neither live with nor support) who supports a qualifying relative in a home they maintain can claim their own basic personal amount, CAD 16,452 for most people, less the dependant’s net income. An infirm dependant adds CAD 2,740 and, at 18 or older, a line 30425 top-up that keeps the total at CAD 8,773 until the dependant’s income passes CAD 20,601. The credit is 14% federally, about CAD 2,303 at most, and only reduces federal tax the claimant actually owes.
For a dependant 18 or older, line 30425 adds the amount by which the lesser of CAD 8,773 and (CAD 29,374 minus their net income) exceeds what was claimed on line 30400.
For an infirm dependant, add CAD 2,740 and complete line 30425 for those 18 or older; for your infirm child under 18, use line 30500.

The 2026 amounts are CRA’s published figures after 2.0% indexation; the CAD 29,374 end point is derived as CAD 8,773 + 20,601, and the same sum for 2025 gives the CAD 28,798 printed on the 2025 form. At 14%, the full CAD 16,452 is worth CAD 2,303.28 of federal tax, and the infirm maximum of CAD 19,192 is worth CAD 2,686.88.

The amount is worked out on Schedule 5. It starts from the claimant’s own basic personal amount, adds CAD 2,740 if the dependant depends on the claimant because of a mental or physical infirmity, and subtracts the dependant’s net income from line 23600:

The credit is non-refundable. It reduces federal tax left after the claimant’s own credits, and any excess is lost: it cannot be carried forward, refunded or moved to anyone else. That matters for single parents on modest incomes, who are the main group this amount is designed for.

The deduction for the dependant’s income cannot take line 30400 below zero. Each CAD 1 claimed is worth 14 cents of federal tax, and only against federal tax the claimant still owes after their own basic personal amount and payroll credits.

The dependant was related to you by blood, marriage, common-law partnership or adoption and was your parent or grandparent; your child, grandchild, brother or sister under 18; or one of those 18 or older with a mental or physical infirmity.

The model is federal only and uses 2026 amounts with the structure of the 2025 schedule. It treats net income as taxable income and estimates the claimant’s federal tax after only the basic personal amount, the Canada employment amount and base CPP and EI credits on employment income. It assumes the eligibility conditions are met and does not test support payments, residency, the part-year separation choice or the disability amount transfer. Provincial and territorial amounts, the Quebec system and the refundable family benefits are not included. Use tax software or the CRA schedule for an actual return.

The third chart shows this cut-off; the grid shows it for five types of dependant. Other credits not modelled, such as tuition, medical expenses or donations, compete for the same tax. Provincial and territorial versions of the amount (line 58160 of Form 428) have their own values and may still be usable. Lower-income single parents get most of their federal support through refundable programs, the Canada child benefit, the GST/HST credit and the Canada workers benefit, which do not depend on this claim.

Without the infirmity, the same parent gives no claim at all. With it, the claim stays at CAD 8,773 until the parent’s income reaches CAD 20,601 and ends at CAD 29,374. “Infirmity” means dependence because of a mental or physical impairment for a considerable period, not a temporary illness or injury. CRA may ask for a medical practitioner’s statement, but not if it already holds an approved Form T2201 disability tax credit certificate for the period.
